title: Pulmonary Nodule: Risk-Stratify Before You Chase It
bottomLine: An incidental pulmonary nodule is managed by malignancy risk, size, morphology, growth and patient factors—not by reflex biopsy or repeated CT without a plan. Symptoms such as hemoptysis or unexplained weight loss move the patient out of a routine screening-style pathway and into diagnostic evaluation.
recognize: Risk rises with smoking exposure, older age, prior cancer, suspicious morphology, upper-lobe location and documented growth.
Many small nodules are benign and require surveillance rather than immediate invasive testing.
differentiate: A nodule found in an asymptomatic screening context is different from a lesion found during evaluation of hemoptysis, weight loss or persistent focal symptoms.
Calcified granuloma patterns can be benign, but prior infection history does not automatically prove benignity.
assessment: Review smoking history, prior malignancy, immune status, TB/fungal exposure, prior imaging, symptoms and patient goals/comorbidity.
Compare with the oldest available imaging before declaring a lesion new or growing.
workup: Use a validated radiology/nodule pathway for surveillance interval and need for PET-CT, specialty referral or tissue diagnosis.
Avoid serial imaging that has no documented endpoint or ownership.
management: Follow low-risk lesions according to the applicable Canadian/provincial radiology pathway and refer higher-risk or growing lesions to lung-cancer/thoracic expertise.
Symptomatic or clearly suspicious lesions require diagnostic workup rather than routine screening follow-up.
medicationSafety: Consider renal function/contrast allergy only when contrast imaging is actually indicated; many surveillance CTs are noncontrast.
Do not delay cancer workup by repeatedly treating presumed infection without objective reassessment when a suspicious lesion persists.
counselling: Explain absolute risk and the reason for surveillance so patients understand why 'watching' can be safer than immediate biopsy.
Support smoking cessation without making cessation a prerequisite for diagnostic care.
followUp: Assign ownership of the next imaging/referral date and close the loop on every recommended surveillance study.
examTrap: Ordering a biopsy for every incidental small nodule—or treating a symptomatic suspicious lesion as if it were merely a screening finding.
oneLinePearl: Nodule care is risk plus growth plus symptoms, with explicit follow-up ownership.
sourceBasis: Canadian lung-nodule and thoracic imaging practice pathways
Cancer Care Ontario lung cancer pathways where applicable

title: Interstitial Lung Disease: Recognize the Pattern and Refer Before Fibrosis Advances
bottomLine: Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, inspiratory crackles and restrictive/diffusion abnormalities should raise ILD concern. Identify medication, occupational, autoimmune and exposure clues, obtain appropriate imaging/PFTs, and refer early rather than treating unexplained interstitial abnormalities as recurrent infection.
recognize: Bibasal fine inspiratory crackles, clubbing, exertional desaturation and restrictive physiology are important clues.
Connective-tissue disease, birds/mould, drugs and occupational exposures can cause secondary ILD.
differentiate: Heart failure, COPD, infection and pulmonary vascular disease can mimic dyspnea and imaging abnormalities.
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude early ILD when clinical suspicion is high.
assessment: Ask tempo, exertional limitation, autoimmune symptoms, smoking, birds/mould, occupation, medications, prior cancer therapy and family history.
Assess oxygenation at rest and with exertion when appropriate.
workup: Use high-resolution CT and full pulmonary function testing when ILD is suspected; order autoimmune/infectious studies only when the differential supports them.
Before immunosuppression, follow current Canadian infection-screening guidance.
management: Refer suspected fibrotic/progressive ILD to respirology/ILD expertise and treat the underlying cause where identifiable.
Pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination, oxygen assessment and smoking cessation support are important adjuncts.
medicationSafety: Antifibrotic and immunosuppressive therapies require diagnosis-specific monitoring and specialist oversight.
Do not begin prolonged steroids for an undifferentiated interstitial pattern before important infectious mimics are considered.
redFlags: Immunosuppressed patient with new diffuse infiltrates
counselling: Explain why establishing the ILD subtype matters because treatments differ substantially.
Discuss exposure avoidance when a credible occupational/environmental driver exists.
followUp: Track symptoms, lung function, oxygen needs and imaging according to specialty guidance; progressive decline warrants treatment-plan reassessment.
examTrap: Repeating antibiotics for progressive dry cough and bilateral interstitial change without considering ILD and exposures.
oneLinePearl: ILD is a pattern to classify early, not a pneumonia label to recycle.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society ILD position statements and guideline library

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Confirm the Disorder, Then Make PAP Usable
bottomLine: OSA is diagnosed with an appropriate sleep study in the right clinical context, not from snoring or a questionnaire alone. Treatment succeeds when PAP or another appropriate therapy is both indicated and usable, with follow-up for residual sleepiness, adherence, mask/pressure problems and driving risk.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, nocturnal choking, resistant hypertension and daytime sleepiness raise probability.
Normal BMI does not exclude OSA.
differentiate: Insomnia, insufficient sleep, circadian disorder, medication effects, depression and central sleep apnea can produce fatigue/sleepiness with different management.
Screening questionnaires estimate probability; they do not establish OSA.
assessment: Assess sleepiness, witnessed events, driving/work risk, sleep duration, alcohol/sedatives, nasal symptoms, cardiometabolic disease and pregnancy when relevant.
workup: Choose home sleep apnea testing versus laboratory polysomnography according to comorbidity, pretest probability and local sleep pathway.
If symptoms remain high-risk after a negative or technically inadequate home test, reassess rather than closing the diagnosis.
management: Use PAP when indicated and address mask fit, humidification, nasal obstruction, pressure intolerance and behavioural barriers.
Oral appliance, positional, surgical or weight-management strategies may be appropriate for selected patients.
medicationSafety: Alcohol, opioids and sedative-hypnotics can worsen sleep-disordered breathing or respiratory risk.
Do not use stimulant therapy to mask untreated OSA without evaluating the cause of persistent sleepiness.
counselling: Discuss driving safety explicitly when sleepiness is significant.
Frame PAP adherence as a troubleshooting problem rather than patient failure.
followUp: Review objective PAP use, residual events/leak, symptoms and cardiometabolic context; persistent symptoms require diagnosis/treatment reassessment.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from a high STOP-BANG score without confirmatory testing—or declaring PAP failure before fixing mask/pressure barriers.
oneLinePearl: Screen for OSA, test for OSA, then make the treatment workable.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society / Canadian Sleep Society resources

title: Pleural Effusion: Is It Fluid Overload, Infection, or Malignancy?
bottomLine: A new pleural effusion is a finding with a cause. Decide whether the presentation fits a known transudative process or requires diagnostic sampling, and escalate infection, respiratory compromise, hemothorax or malignant concern rather than repeatedly diuresing an unexplained unilateral effusion.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain, decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion are common but nonspecific.
Unilateral, large, recurrent or febrile effusions are more likely to require diagnostic evaluation.
differentiate: Heart failure commonly causes bilateral/transudative effusions, but unilateral or atypical effusions deserve broader evaluation.
Parapneumonic effusion/empyema, malignancy, PE and hemothorax change urgency and treatment.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, fever/sepsis, chest pain, malignancy history, heart/liver/renal disease, anticoagulation, trauma and recent procedures.
workup: Use chest imaging/ultrasound to confirm and characterize fluid; diagnostic thoracentesis is selected based on clinical context rather than performed automatically for every small predictable effusion.
When sampled, interpret pleural chemistry, cell count, microbiology and cytology according to the differential.
management: Treat the underlying cause and drain complicated infection, significant symptomatic collections or other indications through the appropriate procedural pathway.
Suspected empyema requires urgent antibiotics plus drainage/source-control planning.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants/bleeding risk before invasive drainage according to current procedural guidance.
Avoid repeated diuretic escalation for an unexplained unilateral effusion without diagnostic reassessment.
counselling: Explain that drainage may be diagnostic, therapeutic or both depending on the cause and symptoms.
followUp: Track radiographic resolution and close the loop on cytology/culture results; recurrent unexplained effusion requires specialty evaluation.
examTrap: Assuming every effusion in a patient with heart failure is simply volume overload despite unilateral recurrence, fever or pleuritic pain.
oneLinePearl: Effusion management starts by asking why the fluid is there.

title: Hemoptysis: Stabilize First, Then Find the Source
bottomLine: Hemoptysis ranges from blood-streaked sputum to a life-threatening airway emergency. First distinguish true pulmonary bleeding from nasopharyngeal/GI sources, then prioritize airway, oxygenation, hemodynamics and bleeding severity before pursuing the cause.
recognize: Bronchiectasis, infection, malignancy, PE and airway disease are important causes; anticoagulation can worsen bleeding without being the underlying diagnosis.
The clinical danger of hemoptysis depends on airway/respiratory compromise and ongoing bleeding, not a memorized millilitre cutoff alone.
differentiate: Hematemesis is usually GI with nausea/coffee-ground material; posterior epistaxis can mimic hemoptysis.
Minor blood-streaked sputum with bronchitis is different from recurrent hemoptysis in a high-risk smoker.
assessment: Assess airway, oxygenation, respiratory rate, hemodynamics, estimated ongoing bleeding, anticoagulants, infection symptoms, cancer/TB risk and pleuritic/PE features.
workup: Use chest imaging and CBC/coagulation studies based on severity and differential; CT/bronchoscopy pathways are selected according to stability and suspected source.
Consider airborne precautions and TB testing when epidemiology/symptoms support it.
management: Unstable or significant ongoing bleeding requires emergency airway/respiratory support and urgent respirology/interventional/thoracic evaluation.
Treat the identified cause; do not merely stop anticoagulation and discharge without source evaluation when bleeding is clinically significant.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants/antiplatelets and reversal need according to severity/indication; thrombosis risk matters too.
Avoid NSAIDs when active clinically significant bleeding increases harm.
counselling: Give explicit emergency-return instructions for recurrent or increasing blood, dyspnea, syncope or chest pain.
followUp: Ensure imaging and specialty follow-up are completed even if bleeding stops when malignancy or structural lung disease remains plausible.
examTrap: Calling hemoptysis 'just anticoagulation' without investigating the pulmonary source.
oneLinePearl: In hemoptysis, protect the airway and explain the bleeding source.
sourceBasis: Canadian respiratory and emergency medicine practice principles
Canadian Tuberculosis Standards where TB is plausible

title: Chronic Cough: Work the Common Causes Without Missing the Dangerous Ones
bottomLine: Chronic cough needs a structured history, medication/exposure review and targeted testing. Upper-airway disease, asthma/eosinophilic airway disease and reflux are common, but hemoptysis, weight loss, abnormal imaging, TB risk, ACE-inhibitor exposure and smoking-related disease change the pathway.
recognize: Cough phenotype, triggers, nocturnal/exertional pattern, sputum and associated upper-airway/reflux/asthma symptoms narrow the differential.
ACE inhibitors can cause chronic cough even after long prior tolerance.
differentiate: Do not diagnose GERD solely because cough is unexplained; empiric trials should have a plausible syndrome and reassessment point.
Chronic cough with abnormal chest imaging, hemoptysis or systemic symptoms requires diagnostic escalation.
assessment: Review smoking/vaping, ACE inhibitor, occupational exposures, nasal symptoms, wheeze, reflux, dysphagia/aspiration, TB risk and red flags.
workup: Use chest radiography and spirometry when appropriate and cause-directed testing thereafter.
Avoid serial antibiotics for chronic cough without evidence of bacterial disease.
management: Stop/replace a likely medication cause when clinically appropriate, treat confirmed upper-airway/asthma/reflux disease and reassess response.
Refer refractory/unexplained cough or abnormal imaging to respiratory/ENT/GI expertise as indicated.
medicationSafety: Chronic codeine/opioid cough suppression adds sedation/dependence risk and can mask progression.
Do not escalate inhaled corticosteroid indefinitely without evidence of an airway phenotype or treatment response.
counselling: Explain that chronic cough often needs sequential hypothesis testing with defined stop/review points rather than multiple simultaneous empiric drugs.
followUp: Document response to each intervention and reconsider the diagnosis when the expected response does not occur.
examTrap: Giving repeated antibiotics to a chronic cough with no bacterial syndrome and no reassessment of medications, asthma or imaging.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough is an algorithm, not an antibiotic refill diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory practice resources
Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory stewardship principles

title: Tuberculosis: Infection, Disease, and Public-Health Action Are Different Problems
bottomLine: A positive TST or IGRA indicates TB infection risk, not active TB disease. Before preventive therapy, exclude active disease; when pulmonary TB is clinically plausible, use appropriate isolation/public-health pathways and obtain microbiologic testing rather than starting latent-TB treatment blindly.
recognize: Persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis and epidemiologic risk raise concern for active pulmonary TB.
Latent TB infection is asymptomatic and noninfectious but carries future progression risk.
differentiate: TST/IGRA cannot distinguish latent infection from active disease.
BCG vaccination affects TST interpretation more than IGRA; test choice depends on age, context and Canadian standards.
assessment: Assess symptoms, prior TB/treatment, birth/residence/travel in high-incidence regions, Indigenous/community context, exposures, immune suppression, pregnancy and medications affecting future regimen choice.
workup: For suspected active pulmonary TB obtain chest imaging and appropriate respiratory specimens for molecular testing, smear/culture and susceptibility according to the Canadian TB pathway.
For asymptomatic infection screening, use TST/IGRA only when there is a clinical/public-health indication and a plan to act on the result.
management: Notify/coordinate with public health as required and use airborne precautions for suspected infectious pulmonary TB according to local protocol.
Treat TB disease and preventive therapy using current Canadian Tuberculosis Standards/regimen-specific guidance rather than memorized legacy courses.
medicationSafety: TB regimens have major hepatic, interaction, ocular and adherence-monitoring considerations; baseline/follow-up testing is regimen and patient specific.
Do not give single-drug latent-TB therapy to someone with unrecognized active disease.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and explain the difference between infection and contagious disease.
Discuss adherence, drug interactions and public-health follow-up clearly.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures/susceptibilities, public-health actions and preventive-treatment completion when indicated.
examTrap: Starting latent-TB treatment after a positive IGRA without first asking whether the patient has active-TB symptoms or abnormal chest imaging.
oneLinePearl: A positive TB infection test is the start of classification, not the diagnosis of active disease.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada TB resources

title: Pulmonary Function Tests: Pattern Before Label
bottomLine: Interpret PFTs as a pattern: confirm acceptable testing, identify obstruction, determine whether low vital capacity represents restriction or air trapping, assess diffusion capacity, and integrate bronchodilator response with the clinical phenotype. One ratio or one 'percent predicted' number does not diagnose the disease by itself.
recognize: Obstruction is an expiratory airflow limitation pattern; restriction requires reduced lung volumes rather than a low FVC alone.
Reduced DLCO can suggest emphysema, ILD, pulmonary vascular disease or anemia depending on the rest of the pattern.
differentiate: Asthma can have normal spirometry between episodes; COPD requires persistent airflow obstruction in the correct exposure/clinical context.
A low FVC with obstruction may reflect air trapping rather than true restriction.
assessment: Confirm test quality, symptoms, smoking/exposures, inhaler timing, neuromuscular/chest-wall factors and hemoglobin context for diffusion interpretation.
workup: Use post-bronchodilator spirometry when needed, full lung volumes for suspected restriction and DLCO when the differential warrants it.
Compare trends using appropriate reference equations rather than treating small numerical changes as definite clinical deterioration.
management: Use the physiologic pattern to guide the next diagnostic step or therapy; refer discordant/complex restriction, diffusion impairment or unexplained dyspnea to respiratory expertise.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate inhaled therapy solely because a spirometry value is abnormal without confirming diagnosis, technique, adherence and phenotype.
counselling: Explain that PFTs describe physiology and need the clinical story to identify the cause.
followUp: Repeat testing only when the result will change diagnosis, treatment or monitoring of a known disease.
examTrap: Calling low FVC 'restrictive lung disease' without lung-volume confirmation—or diagnosing COPD from symptoms without objective obstruction.
oneLinePearl: PFTs name the physiologic pattern; the clinician names the disease.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society pulmonary function testing resources
Current ATS/ERS lung-function interpretation standards used in Canadian practice

title: Oxygen Therapy: Treat Documented Hypoxemia, Not Dyspnea Alone
bottomLine: Oxygen is a drug. Acute oxygen should target clinically appropriate saturation goals, and long-term/home oxygen requires documented qualifying hypoxemia or another evidence-based indication—not breathlessness alone. Reassess oxygen needs after an acute illness rather than assuming a temporary prescription is lifelong.
recognize: Hypoxemia and dyspnea are related but not synonymous; anxiety, heart failure, anemia and deconditioning can cause severe dyspnea with normal oxygenation.
Some patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure require controlled oxygen targets and close reassessment.
differentiate: Short-term oxygen during an acute exacerbation is different from long-term oxygen therapy for stable chronic hypoxemia.
Ambulatory/nocturnal oxygen indications require documented physiology and disease-specific evidence rather than symptom preference alone.
assessment: Assess oxygen saturation in context, work of breathing, ABG/VBG when hypercapnia is a concern, baseline oxygen use, smoking/fire risk and the underlying disease.
workup: For chronic/home oxygen, document qualifying resting/exertional/nocturnal hypoxemia according to the applicable Canadian/provincial pathway and reassess after stabilization.
Investigate unexplained new oxygen need rather than treating the number without finding the cause.
management: Titrate acute oxygen to an appropriate clinical target and treat the underlying cause of hypoxemia.
For long-term therapy, prescribe device/flow/use conditions through the applicable respiratory/home-oxygen program and reassess ongoing need.
medicationSafety: Fire risk with smoking/open flame is critical home-oxygen safety teaching.
Excess uncontrolled oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible patients; oxygen should be titrated and monitored rather than withheld when genuinely hypoxemic.
redFlags: New oxygen dependence after acute illness without reassessment plan
counselling: Teach device use, fire safety, travel planning and when increasing oxygen need requires urgent review.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, saturation/gas exchange and ongoing eligibility after acute recovery or major disease change.
examTrap: Prescribing long-term oxygen because a patient is very breathless despite normal oxygen saturation—or withholding oxygen from a hypoxemic COPD patient because of fear of CO2 retention.
oneLinePearl: Oxygen treats hypoxemia and must be prescribed, targeted and reassessed like any other drug.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society home oxygen and COPD respiratory support resources

title: Lung Cancer Screening: High-Risk Screening Is Not Symptom Workup
bottomLine: Low-dose CT lung-cancer screening is for asymptomatic people who meet a current organized-program high-risk pathway. Hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, suspicious imaging or persistent focal symptoms require diagnostic evaluation instead of waiting for the next screening round.
recognize: Eligibility varies by province/territory and can use organized risk-assessment models rather than one universal Canada-wide age/pack-year rule.
Screening finds nodules that then require structured risk-based follow-up; the screening CT is not the end of the care pathway.
differentiate: Screening = asymptomatic high-risk population testing; diagnostic CT/workup = symptoms or a concerning known finding.
A person can benefit from smoking-cessation support whether or not they currently meet screening eligibility.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, then smoking exposure, prior cancer, comorbidity, ability/willingness to undergo downstream diagnosis/treatment and local screening access.
workup: Use the current provincial/territorial organized screening referral pathway; in Ontario, eligibility is determined through the Ontario Lung Screening Program risk assessment.
Use diagnostic imaging/pathways rather than screening referral when symptoms are present.
management: Refer eligible asymptomatic high-risk patients to the organized screening program and ensure abnormal findings receive the recommended diagnostic follow-up.
Offer evidence-based smoking-cessation treatment without making cessation a condition of screening or diagnostic care.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary antibiotic or steroid trials that delay evaluation of a suspicious lesion or symptom pattern.
Consider contrast/renal issues only when the downstream diagnostic test requires contrast; screening LDCT itself is generally noncontrast.
counselling: Discuss potential benefit, false positives, incidental findings and the possibility of downstream procedures.
Explain that screening is not a substitute for evaluation when symptoms develop.
followUp: Track every abnormal screen until its recommended imaging or diagnostic endpoint is completed.
examTrap: Referring a patient with new hemoptysis into a routine lung-screening pathway instead of initiating diagnostic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms means screening; symptoms mean diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario Ontario Lung Screening Program
Canadian provincial/territorial lung cancer screening programs
